abstract: Conceptus elongation is a shared feature of preimplantation development in roe deer and cattle. However, unlike cattle embryos, roe deer embryos undergo embryonic diapause prior to elongation, during which blastocyst growth remains markedly reduced for 4-5 months before development rapidly resumes. To investigate the molecular basis of these developmental differences, we assembled a novel roe deer reference genome and analyzed single-embryo transcriptomes from diapausing and elongated roe deer conceptuses, comparing their transcriptomes with those of cattle embryos from day 6 morulae to day 14 tubular conceptuses. Pseudotime and principal component analyses revealed parallel developmental trajectories across species and distinct gene-expression profiles during diapause. Roe deer diapause embryos exhibited reduced transcriptional signatures of oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial biogenesis and protein glycosylation pathways relative to cattle blastocysts, while maintaining expression of lineage-specification markers, consistent with continued differentiation despite a metabolically quiescent state. While roe deer retained the function of the corpus luteum during diapause and continued to secrete progesterone, they did not express interferon-{tau} upon elongation. Elongation of roe deer embryos triggered robust upregulation of cell-cycle regulators, ribosomal biogenesis and oxidative-phosphorylation genes, aligning with the high energetic demands of elongation. By contrasting a diapause and non-diapause species, we illuminated the genomic and metabolic frameworks that underlie this unique reproductive adaptation of diapause and elongation.
